title: Perplexity Launches Orchestrator API for Failover and Model Routing
summary: Perplexity’s Orchestrator API serves OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and open-weight models through 1 endpoint, with same-model provider failover, unified billing and a preview perplexity/auto router that sends each request to a described route. The post Perplexity Launches Orchestrator API for Failover and Model Routing appeared first on MarkTechPost .
content: Perplexity has launched the Perplexity Orchestrator API , a single endpoint for frontier and open-weight models. It picks a serving provider by availability, capacity and latency , and bills everything through 1 account. Developers get fewer integrations and 1 invoice. What is the Perplexity Orchestrator API? The Perplexity Orchestrator API is a hosted inference gateway that serves many models behind 1 base URL. It covers frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI . It also serves open-weight models such as GLM, Kimi and DeepSeek, hosted by Perplexity or inference partners. It accepts OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages requests. Most teams only change the API key and base URL. The OpenAI base URL is https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator/v1 . Anthropic SDK users point at https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator , without /v1 . Perplexity runs the same layer internally, across 85+ models and more than a dozen providers. How does provider failover work? Failover keeps the model fixed and swaps the deployment. A Claude request that fails on Anthropic can be served by AWS Bedrock instead. The reliability docs set these rules: Triggers are provider errors, rate limits and timeouts. Each attempt has a time-to-first-token limit and a total-duration limit. The values are not published. Invalid or over-context requests return HTTP 400 and are not retried. If every deployment fails, the API returns HTTP 429 with Retry-After . Requests that fail before producing output are not billed. You cannot pick a deployment yourself. What do the reliability and speed numbers show? Perplexity measured production traffic from October 4 to November 2, 2026. Claude and GPT requests through Perplexity succeeded more often than requests to any single provider measured. Daily success rates also varied less during provider incidents. The post gives no percentage success rates. Speed varied by provider too. For Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic was fastest on 15 of 30 days, AWS Bedrock on 15. Azure’s median output speed for GPT-5.6 Sol was 27% higher than OpenAI’s. Speed-aware routing is still in progress. How does automatic routing with perplexity/auto work? Routing is in preview. You set model to perplexity/auto and pass a routing object. It holds a default_model and 1 to 5 routes , each with a name, description and model. A decision model reads the conversation and route descriptions. It never sees route names or model IDs. If nothing matches, or the decision model fails or times out, the default model answers. So do media inputs. Response headers report the result: x-perplexity-autoroute-outcome , -route and -confidence . The default policy sends traffic to GPT-6.1 Sol, with simple requests going to GPT-6 Luna. Perplexity also lists built-in Lower cost, Balanced and Higher quality profiles, plus an Auto effort preview. && Can routing work around refusals? Perplexity tested this on a 63-task subset of Terminal-Bench 4.1 , run in Claude Code. Anthropic documents that Claude Fable 5.2 safeguards can block benign security and life sciences work. Claude Fable 5.2 alone: 38/63 tasks. Fable plus routes to GPT-6.1 Sol: 41/63. Fable plus routes to GPT-6 Astra: 41/63. The routes covered security , biology and after_refusal requests. That is +3 tasks, at a higher estimated cost per task. Perplexity calls it an adjusted comparison; results vary by workload. How is Orchestrator priced? Each request is billed at the answering model’s published per-token rate. Failover to another provider does not change the rate. Perplexity says there is no additional platform fee on top of credits . For example, perplexity/glm-5.3 lists $1.4 input, $4.4 output and $0.26 cache read per 1M tokens . Usage draws from prepaid Perplexity API credits, also purchasable through AWS Marketplace. Access is tiered by cumulative credit purchases : Tier 0: Google, xAI and open-weight models. Tier 1 ($50): OpenAI and most Anthropic models. Tier 2 ($250): Claude Opus 5, Opus 5.5 and the Fable models. How does it compare with OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway? Feature Perplexity Orchestrator OpenRouter Vercel AI Gateway Model catalog Frontier (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI) plus open-weight GLM, Kimi, DeepSeek; count not disclosed ( blog ) 400+ models, 70+ providers ( source ) 400+ models ( source ) API formats Chat Completions, Responses, Anthropic Messages ( docs ) Chat Completions, Responses, Anthropic Messages ( docs ) Chat Completions, Responses, Anthropic Messages ( docs ) Platform fee No additional platform fee on credits ( blog ) 5.5% on credit purchases (Standard), 8% (Business) ( pricing ) No platform fee, no token markup ( pricing ) Token pricing Answering model’s published rate ( FAQ ) Provider price passed through ( FAQ ) Provider list price ( docs ) Same-model provider failover Yes, automatic ( docs ) Yes, automatic fallback ( source ) Yes, automatic ( changelog ) Prompt-based auto router perplexity/auto , preview, 1 to 5 routes ( docs ) openrouter/auto , no router fee ( docs ) Not disclosed Bring your own key Not supported ( FAQ ) Supported, 5% fee above allowance ( FAQ ) Supported, no markup ( docs ) Key Takeaways 1 endpoint for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and open-weight models. Same-model failover across providers, billed at the same rate. perplexity/auto routes by plain-language descriptions, in preview. Refusal routing: 38/63 to 41/63 on Terminal-Bench 4.1, self-reported. title: Not If, But How: Responding to Security Incidents in the Age of AI Attackers
summary: AI-powered attackers are driving more frequent attacks on AI infrastructure. This guide reviews 6 months of incidents, sets out a 4-pillar incident response playbook, and shows it in practice through Fireworks AI and Klue. The post Not If, But How: Responding to Security Incidents in the Age of AI Attackers appeared first on MarkTechPost .
content: Attackers now have powerful AI on their side. AI agents can scan, plan and run intrusions at machine speed, and they improve every month. The result is more attacks, more often and at global scale. In that environment, more companies will face a security incident at some point. What separates them is how they respond. Machine-speed threats call for a modern playbook with 4 pillars. Detect and contain automatically. Communicate fast and securely. Eradicate thoroughly. Keep shrinking the blast radius. This article shows the trend through 6 months of incidents. It then looks at a few companies, with Fireworks AI as a model of mature, structurally sound response. TL;DR The trend: AI-powered attackers are driving more frequent attacks at global scale. The evidence: Several AI platforms disclosed security incidents between May and November 2026. Pillar 1: Detect and contain automatically. Human-speed shutdowns are too slow. Pillar 2: Communicate fast and securely, over out-of-band channels. Pillar 3: Eradicate thoroughly, with outside forensic experts. Pillar 4: Keep shrinking the blast radius. Data that is never stored cannot be stolen. Case studies: Fireworks AI and Klue show these pillars in practice. Why are attacks becoming more frequent? AI has changed the economics of attacking. Tasks that took skilled people days can now be delegated to agents. In November, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said AI misuse had reached a “critical inflection point” . They report that attackers use AI to shorten timelines and run multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. CrowdStrike reported that 1 group used AI agents against more than 200 organizations in 11 days . Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 found attacks moving about 4 times faster than a year earlier. The shift started earlier. In 2025, Anthropic disrupted a campaign where AI did 80 to 90% of tactical work with little human input. The tools keep improving, so the pace will keep rising. AI infrastructure is an especially attractive target, because AI access itself has value. The last 6 months show what that looks like. What was disclosed in the last 6 months? Incidents appeared across every layer of the AI stack. Together they show how broad the activity has become. May: package registries. On May 10 and 11, the “Mini Shai-Hulud” campaign altered about 170 npm packages and some PyPI libraries . Affected projects included AI SDKs from Mistral AI and Guardrails AI. The NHS cyber alert lists the specific versions to avoid. June: SaaS integrations. Klue, a market intelligence platform, disclosed misuse of OAuth tokens it held for customers. See case study 2. August: self-hosted AI gateways. Microsoft described intrusions into exposed, unpatched LiteLLM, RAGFlow and Kestra deployments. Fixed versions exist for all 3 tools . CISA had listed the LiteLLM flaw as known exploited on June 8. September: evaluation environments. Anthropic’s September threat report described attempts to obtain AI keys through software vendors. The Cloud Security Alliance summarized it . In 1 case, instructions were injected into a vendor’s automated evaluation sandbox. October and early November: developer platforms. At least 9 AI developer and hosting platforms disclosed incidents involving stored customer secrets in October. Wiz’s tracker later listed further disclosures, for 16 platforms in total. A tampered LiteLLM release, version 1.107.0, was also identified , and users were told to roll back. November: shared web vendors. On November 16, an attacker abused a flaw in Optimizely’s account signup flow to inject code into customer projects, reaching 178 organizations’ websites, according to Report URI, including HSBC, Salesforce, the BBC and Ledger. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses and skimmed payment forms; Optimizely removed the payload and fixed the flaw. Hudson Rock traced similar code through three other web services, beginning November 13. It is the same concentration pattern, one layer below the AI stack. Date (2026) Platform What was affected Entry point, as reported May 10 to 11 npm and PyPI packages, incl. Mistral AI and Guardrails AI SDKs Developer and CI credentials on installing hosts Poisoned package releases June 11 to 12 Klue Customer Salesforce and Gong data Legacy credential, then stored OAuth tokens August LiteLLM, RAGFlow, Kestra deployments Model provider keys, backend access Exposed, unpatched gateways October 6 Fireworks AI Environment variables in evaluation jobs, limited accounts Misused internal credentials October 14 to 15 Zeabur 3,218,965 environment variable records, 321,810 accounts Long-lived admin tokens, exposed admin interface October 15 Lightning AI Credentials; Studio taken offline Credential access October 16 to 17 OpenCode OpenAI, Anthropic and Google keys of about 1.4% of Console users Legacy system October 20 to 21 Railway Encrypted environment variables, some decrypted Privilege escalation in build infrastructure October 21 LiteLLM 1.107.0 Cloud credentials and LLM keys on installing hosts Release pipeline compromise October 23 Warp Agent decision logs and telemetry, about 1% of users Third-party vendor dependency October 23 to 24 Fireworks AI Billing data; for some customers, datasets and incomplete model weights Incident at a third-party cloud provider October 29 Cursor Altered extension copy in its marketplace cache, up to 5,000 users Credential from exposed internal data October 30 Northflank Customers told to assume environment variables were decrypted Not disclosed November 8 NEAR AI Inference server; 2 API keys exposed in logs Remote code execution flaw in SGLang Selected incidents: Dates follow the linked sources, which sometimes differ by a day. Several October entries rely on compilations by Wiz and Helix rather than primary vendor disclosures. What do these incidents have in common? There was no single vulnerability. According to the Cloud Security Alliance, entry points varied . The common target was stored environment variables, often holding AI provider API keys. AI keys carry real value, which explains the interest. CSA, citing Anthropic, notes that a key can be resold, used for compute or used as cover . Wiz estimated that misuse of 2 keys from these incidents exceeded $100,000 at list price . That is why spending caps matter. Concentration is the other shared factor. A platform that stores secrets for many customers naturally draws attention. CSA describes this as the platform-chain pattern . What does a modern incident response playbook look like? No company can promise it will never be breached. Every company can control how it responds. Against attackers that move at machine speed, that response rests on 4 pillars. 1. Detect and contain automatically: A human-speed shutdown is no longer enough. An AI-driven intruder can move between systems in minutes. Mature teams wire detection directly to containment. That means kill-switches, automatic token revocation and host isolation. Wiz recommends alerting on bulk secret reads , the clearest signal in this year’s incidents. The best setups act on that signal automatically. 2. Communicate fast, and securely: Speed still matters most for revocation. Customers need to rotate keys, and upstream providers need to revoke access at the source. CSA notes that deleting a key from a platform does not revoke it . Mature teams also choose the channel with care. A Five Eyes joint advisory warns against communicating over the network under investigation . It advises out-of-band communication instead. CISA’s playbooks likewise call for out-of-band communications infrastructure as part of preparation. That keeps an attacker who is still watching from learning the response plan. 3. Eradicate thoroughly: Closing the hole that was used is only the first step. Top teams assume the attacker planted backdoors and hunt for them. They bring in independent forensic experts, such as Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 or Mandiant. The same advisory recommends third-party incident response support . It also warns against fixing symptoms instead of the root cause. 4. Keep improving by shrinking the blast radius: Attackers improve every month, so security is never finished. The strongest proactive defense limits what any future attacker can reach. Zero Trust access means no credential is trusted by default. Ephemeral architecture means sensitive data is not kept at all. If data isn’t stored, it can’t be stolen. Some companies already apply these pillars. The 2 case studies below show how: Case study 1: How did Fireworks AI respond? Fireworks AI is an inference and training platform. It disclosed an incident in October, 2026, during a busy month for the industry. Its response is a strong example of mature, structurally sound incident response across the 4 pillars. Pillar 1: detect and contain Fireworks identified unauthorized use of internal credentials on October 6 . A second event began on October 24, through a third-party cloud provider that hosted its R&D machines. Fireworks detected that activity and closed it on the same day it began. That is the kind of operational agility machine-speed threats demand. Pillar 2: communicate fast Fireworks began notifying affected customers on October 7 , about 1 day after detection . It published a public bulletin on October 9 and has updated it as findings came in. It also notified law enforcement. The bulletin lists affected resource metadata and billing information. For certain customers, it also lists datasets, incomplete model weights and secrets. Pillar 3: eradicate thoroughly Fireworks engaged Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for forensic analysis. Bringing in an independent, top-tier team is a mature decision. It means the investigation looks beyond the first entry point, for anything an attacker may have left behind. Fireworks also completed rotation of employee API keys by October 9 . Pillar 4: a smaller blast radius by design Fireworks’ most important protection was already in place. It says it detected no impact to its Inference, Training SDK and Nexus products. All 3 run with zero data retention by default, so prompts and outputs are not stored at rest. That architecture kept the core products out of the reported impact. Fireworks has since gone further. It paused its Batch API , and its documentation says stored Batch inputs and outputs will be permanently deleted. Enterprise customers can also enforce an account-wide ZDR policy . The philosophy behind it: On November 13, 2026, Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao posted on X to explain the company’s data retention policy. She described 2 standard API designs: Customer-managed retention (upload, use, delete). A user uploads a dataset, runs jobs on it, then deletes it. Batch APIs are the typical example. The platform keeps the data until told to delete it, because it cannot know when the user is finished. Cleanup is the user’s job. Fireworks says it does not retain data after deletion. Ephemeral processing (send, compute, return). The platform processes a request and returns the result without keeping the content. This is zero data retention. Fireworks applies it to its inference APIs, its Training SDK, including serverless training, and Nexus. Prompts and generations are not persisted at rest. She compared it to saving a spreadsheet in a cloud drive versus passing its numbers to a calculator. In both designs, customers control their data. Her conclusion is that ephemeral processing is preferable whenever the workflow allows it. It leaves no forgotten datasets or missed deletion calls, and every retained copy is something to protect. In our view, this is the gold standard for proactive defense, and the October events bear it out. Some customers, including Cursor, Uber and Notion, have published their own notices. Investigations are ongoing. The lesson: same-day containment, fast notice and independent forensics limit an incident’s duration. Ephemeral architecture limits what can be reached at all. Case study 2: How did Klue respond? Klue is a market intelligence platform that connects to customer CRM and sales tools. Its June incident shows the same habits in a different part of the stack. What happened. On June 11 and 12, an attacker used a compromised legacy credential tied to Klue’s integration service. With it, they obtained OAuth tokens Klue held for customers. Those tokens were used to read data from some connected Salesforce and Gong environments. Pillars 1 and 2: detect and communicate. Klue identified the activity on June 12 and notified customers the same day . Same-day notice let customers start reviewing their own connected systems at once. Pillars 1 and 3: contain and eradicate. Klue revoked affected credentials and disabled 9 integrations, including Salesforce, HubSpot, Gong and Slack. Salesforce disabled the Klue integration on June 17 . The lesson: every stored token is standing access. Retiring old credentials and long-lived tokens is pillar 4 in practice for integration platforms. What do the two case studies have in common? Both companies held something on behalf of customers: datasets and secrets at Fireworks, OAuth tokens at Klue. Both detected the activity and notified customers within about a day. Both cut off access at the source. Fireworks went further on pillars 3 and 4, with independent forensics and an architecture that stores less by default. Who is responsible when an AI platform has an incident? Usually more than 1 party. Most of these events ran through a chain of companies, and each link plays a role. Upstream suppliers: Cloud providers, package registries and build tools sit beneath every platform. Fireworks’ second event began at a third-party cloud provider . The May package campaign and the LiteLLM release began in build and publishing pipelines . The platform or provider: A platform that holds customer secrets is responsible for protecting them. CSA calls platform operators a main point of control . The vendor building on the platform: Companies that integrate an AI API decide what they send, store and share. When they use upload-based features, deleting data they no longer need is part of their job. In Cursor’s case, the key opened a bucket Cursor used to share data with Fireworks . Some traces in it held unredacted credentials, which reached Cursor’s own tools. Cursor has since added secret scanning and rotated its credentials. The end customer: Keys stay valid until the issuing provider revokes them. CSA suggests treating each long-lived key as exposed if a platform holding it reports an incident . Good choices at any link can contain an incident. That is why the guidance below is split by role. What do the incidents show about stored data? A useful lesson comes from what was not affected. Cursor reports that prompts and code from Privacy Mode users were not affected . That data was never kept, so there was nothing to copy. The pattern holds across the timeline. Incidents involved stored items: environment variables, OAuth tokens, datasets, logs and traces. Live requests processed in memory were not among the reported impacts. This is the practical case for ephemeral processing. Fewer stored copies mean fewer things to protect, track and delete. What should each party do next? The guidance below draws on CSA, Wiz and government incident response advice. AI providers and platforms Deploy automated containment triggers for bulk secret reads. Revoke tokens and isolate workloads without waiting for a human. Retire non-expiring admin tokens, and keep admin interfaces off the public internet. Separate internal workloads from customer workloads. Set up out-of-band communication channels before an incident, and use them during it. Notify customers, partners, upstream providers and law enforcement quickly. Measure notice time in hours. Retain an independent forensic firm in advance, so eradication can start on day 1. Adopt ephemeral architecture and zero data retention wherever workflows allow. Offer spending caps and short-lived credentials by default. Vendors building on AI APIs Prefer ephemeral, zero data retention endpoints. As Lin Qiao puts it, use them whenever the workflow allows . When you do upload data, own the delete step. Set expiry dates on shared buckets and datasets, and delete them when the job ends. Scan prompts, traces and datasets for secrets before they leave your systems. Issue 1 key per platform and per application, so revocation stays narrow. Ask suppliers how fast they detect, contain and notify, and whether they use outside forensics. Every team holding AI keys Rotate at the issuing provider. Deleting a key from a platform does not revoke it . Set spending and rate caps that match expected use. Review usage and billing logs after any supplier notice. Key Takeaways AI-powered attackers are making attacks faster, more frequent and more global. Modern response rests on 4 pillars: contain automatically, communicate securely, eradicate thoroughly, shrink the blast radius. Zero data retention kept companies like Fireworks’ core products out of the reported impact. If data isn’t stored, it can’t be stolen. title: Google DeepMind Releases Gemini 4 Neon: 1M Context, #1 on AA Coding Agent Index
summary: Google released Gemini 4 Neon, a 1M-context Gemini 4 model priced at $3/$15 per million tokens. It scores 61 on the AA Intelligence Index and ranks #1 on AA’s Coding Agent Index. The post Google DeepMind Releases Gemini 4 Neon: 1M Context, #1 on AA Coding Agent Index appeared first on MarkTechPost .
content: Google DeepMind just released Gemini 4 Neon . Gemini 4 Neon is a reasoning model that sits between Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen. It targets coding agents, knowledge work and science workflows. The developer pitch is near-frontier scores at a lower cost per task. Pricing is $3 per 1M input tokens and $15 per 1M output tokens. TL;DR Size: 1M-token unified context, 64K default output, up to 1M via background long decode. Runs on: Google-hosted only. Closed weights, so no local GPU, quantized or edge builds. Performance: 61 on the AA Intelligence Index, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (59) and GPT-6.2 Sol (57). Best: 95.2% on GraphWalks (256K to 1M context), vs 80.1% for GPT-6.2 Sol. Worst: 46.2% on FrontierCode 2.0, behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 47.3%. Bottom line: Best: leads long-context and agentic coding at $3/$15. Worst: closed, self-reported, pricier per token than GPT-6.2 Sol. What is Gemini 4 Neon? Neon is the middle model in the Gemini 4 family. Carbon handles the hardest long-horizon projects. Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution. Neon balances depth and efficiency between the two. As per the model card , Neon is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon. Google does not disclose parameter count or architecture. Inputs cover text, images, audio and video. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026. How does Neon work inside agent workflows? Neon exposes multiple thinking levels. High is the default. xhigh is reserved for the hardest engineering, analytical and science workloads. For long agent runs, Neon supports context compaction and makes fewer redundant file reads. In Google Antigravity , Neon can act as an orchestrator. It directs parallel Gemini 4 Hydrogen subagents on smaller subtasks. How does Gemini 4 Neon perform on benchmarks? Google compares Neon against Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol. All scores below are reported by Google, not independently reproduced. Coding: #1 on the AA Coding Agent Index at 58.6. SWE-sweep with provider harness hits 39.0%, vs 10.1% for Opus 5.5. Knowledge work: 56.3% on Zapier AutomationBench , vs 42.5% for Opus 5.5. 75.8% on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 . Science and reasoning: 84.0% on RiemannBench , 70.5% on Terminal-Bench-Science and 71.3% on HLE-Diamond . Long context: 95.2% on GraphWalks, vs 66.8% for Opus 5.5. Cyber: 90.5% on SEC-bench Pro , 70.7% on CWE-Bench v2 and 51.3% on WebExploitBench v1.2. Neon does not win every row. Opus 5.5 leads Terminal-bench 4.1 (65.8% vs 65.2%) and FrontierCode 2.0 (47.3% vs 46.2%). GPT-6.2 Sol leads Chartography (75.1% vs 73.5%). On the Vals Index , Neon scores 70.9% and ranks #2. On the Agent Arena index it also ranks #2, with a score of 1336. &&& What does Gemini 4 Neon cost? Neon lists at $3 input, $0.15 cached input and $15 output per 1M tokens. Google says Neon at high thinking costs 32% less per task than Carbon. It also claims 50% to 80% lower cost per task vs rivals on Vals Index and Agent Arena. At xhigh, Google cites 36%+ lower cost than rivals at their highest settings. Those are per-task claims, not per-token prices. GPT-6.2 Sol lists at $2/$10. Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4/$20. Gemini 4 Carbon is $2/$10 until November 30, then $4/$20. Where can developers use Gemini 4 Neon? Gemini API paid tier, via Google AI Studio and Android Studio Gemini for business , via API and the model dropdown Google Antigravity, for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers The Gemini app , for Pro and Ultra subscribers What do the safety numbers show? Neon runs on the Gemini 4 safety and security stack . Google reports a 0.09% misaligned action rate on its agentic safety suite. It passes 99.2% of the agent honesty evaluation. It shows a 0.0% attack success rate on Gray Swan’s prompt injection benchmark at the highest thinking level. Its 2.45% shortcut rate on a coding cheating test is the lowest of any Gemini 4 model. title: Nutrient Data Extraction API: JSON Matching Your Schema With Per-Field Citations and Confidence
summary: Nutrient Data Extraction API parses PDFs, scans and Office files into JSON matching your schema. Fields carry page, region and match-label citations, and Studio lets teams test before writing code. The post Nutrient Data Extraction API: JSON Matching Your Schema With Per-Field Citations and Confidence appeared first on MarkTechPost .
content: An LLM presents you a wrong value extracted from a document as fact. That error is costly, especially when basing decisions on it. The Nutrient Data Extraction API targets that problem. It parses PDFs, scans, images and Office files into spatial JSON or Markdown. Extract maps fields from a document onto your JSON schema, and split, classify and form endpoints provide useful primitives for your document pipelines. Each extracted value is anchored to a page via a bounding box, a match label and a confidence score. Nutrient (formerly PSPDFKit) runs the same engine behind an MCP server , agent skill, Mac app and SDK . TL;DR Size: A hosted API with 4 parse modes plus auto routing. Runs on: Nutrient cloud, your own servers via SDK, or an Apple silicon Mac. Where to try it: Studio , a browser workspace to configure and test parsing, extraction,classification, splitting, and form filling. Performance: 86.2 overall on Nutrient’s WholeDoc Bench , top of 19 settings (live API, Agentic). Best: 86.2 at 1.8¢ per page, versus 67.1 at 17.8¢ for the best frontier-model setting. How do you test it in Studio before writing code? Studio is Nutrient’s browser workspace for configuring and testing the API before integrating it in your application. It enables you to test parsing, extraction, classification , splitting, and form filling on your own files. A typical loop: Upload a sample document and set the parameters you plan to send. Draft a schema in the UI, or generate one based on your own documents. Run it on a fresh document, then inspect values and citations. Save the setup as a versioned preset. The API calls it a processor , with a proc_ ID. Score preset versions against up to 25 reviewed documents in an evaluation set. Processors saved in Studio can then be called from the API by ID. Which mode should you pick? Auto routes each page to structure , understand or agentic . If the mode is omitted, the API defaults to understand . Operation Best for Price per page Extract per page WholeDoc Bench* Parse: text Born-digital PDFs and Office files, no OCR $0.001 $0.007** Not tested Parse: structure OCR for scans with simple layouts, no AI $0.0015 $0.0075 39.4 Parse: understand AI layout analysis: forms, complex layouts $0.009 $0.015 80.8 Parse: agentic Vision language model: cursive, degraded scans, charts $0.018 $0.024 86.2 Classify Zero-shot document labels $0.001 n/a n/a Split Separating merged PDFs into documents $0.003 n/a n/a * WholeDoc Bench parsing score, 5 November 2026; not extraction accuracy. Extract adds $0.006 per page. **API docs list text-mode extract; the agent skill starts at structure. Pricing is in dollars, from 1 balance shared across Nutrient’s cloud APIs, so teams can mix and match. The free plan gives you $5 monthly usage that covers about 330 understand-mode extractions. Starter costs $75 a month for $90 of usage; Growth costs $275 for $345. How does grounded confidence work? In Nutrient’s confidence post , a field scored 0.97 but came from the wrong column. The current score is a composite of optional signals: token probability, candidate margin, grounding and format. Nutrient’s NLI grounding model is open under Apache-2.0. A grounded value can still answer the wrong field. When no score exists, confidence is omitted, not low. Each field also gets a match label: id_match, id_match_multiblock, id_match_partial, fuzzy_match or not_found. Gate on the label first, then confidence. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser import json, requests API_KEY = "your_api_key" schema = { "type": "object", "properties": { "invoice_number": {"type": "string", "description": "Invoice number below the supplier details."}, "total_amount": {"type": "number", "description": "Printed final total including tax. Not the subtotal."}, }, "required": ["invoice_number", "total_amount"], } instructions = {"schema": schema, "parseConfig": {"mode": "understand"}, "options": {"includeCitations": True}} with open("invoice.pdf", "rb") as f: r = requests.post( "https://api.nutrient.io/extraction/extract", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}, files={"file": ("invoice.pdf", f, "application/pdf"), "instructions": (None, json.dumps(instructions), "application/json")}, timeout=300, ) r.raise_for_status() out = r.json()["output"] data, metadata = out.get("data") or {}, out.get("metadata") or {} EXACT = {"id_match", "id_match_multiblock"} THRESHOLD = 0.97 # illustrative only; evaluate on representative documents for field in schema["properties"]: # loop over expected fields so none skip review value = data.get(field) meta = metadata.get(field) or {} match, conf = meta.get("match"), meta.get("confidence") # None = no score passes = (value is not None and match in EXACT and conf is not None and conf >= THRESHOLD) print(field, value, match, conf, "page", meta.get("pageNumber"), "PASSES_BASIC_CHECKS" if passes else "REVIEW") This demo covers flat schemas only; production needs type and business-rule checks. The 0.97 bar mirrors money fields in Nutrient’s mortgage tutorial . How do classify and split work? A document decision model powers classify and split . Nutrient reports 96.2% split F1 against 63.7% for Typesafe AI’s Jev. How do agents use it? The hosted MCP server needs no API key. Claude Code connects with 1 command: Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser claude mcp add --transport http --scope user nutrient https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp Claude and Codex also work via OAuth. Default agentic mode costs $0.018 per page to parse. Coding agents can install the document-extraction-api skill with npx skills add pspdfkit-labs/nutrient-skills –skill document-extraction-api. Can it run locally? On the Mac app, documents stay local only with a local model. Fully offline production needs the SDK . How does it score on WholeDoc Bench? Nutrient’s new WholeDoc Bench scores whole documents, not single pages: 480 documents, 30+ languages, 7 areas. Setting Overall Tables Charts Position ¢/page Nutrient Agentic 86.2 87.1 64.5 88.6 1.8 Nutrient Understand 80.8 86.1 35.1 86.4 0.9 Claude Fable 5.1 (high effort) 67.1 84.7 58.9 66.0 17.8 Azure Document Intelligence 65.9 69.4 0 72.5 ≈2.8 GPT-6.1 Sol (medium effort) 62.9 82.8 47.6 49.3 ≈3.1 Extend (performance) 60.5 80.8 40.6 75.2 2.0 Reducto (R-1) 59.9 76.4 38.5 76.4 ≈1.7 LlamaParse Agentic Plus 56.7 89.5 0* 65.4 ≈5.6 AWS Textract 49.9 71.4 0 70.0 1.5 Docling 40.0 63.9 20.2 0 Local Selected rows, WholeDoc leaderboard , 5 November 2026, list prices. *Score still under review. Cross-page continuity is the biggest gap. On 44 documents with page-spanning tables, 15 of 19 settings rarely kept them whole. Nutrient built and ran it, and the main test set is private. The code is Apache-2.0, with a 10-document public sample. Key Takeaways Fields carry pages, regions, match labels and, when available, confidence. Configure and test in Studio before writing any API code. Understand-mode extraction costs $15 per 1,000 pages. Agentic tops Nutrient’s WholeDoc Bench at 86.2 for 1.8¢ per page. Charts remain hard: 64.5 is the best WholeDoc chart score. See the Data Extraction API , benchmarks , MCP server and agent skill on GitHub . title: New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65%
summary: Hugging Face released Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted, an Apache-2.0 LoRA adapter trained with reinforcement learning for the pi coding agent. It lifts SWE-bench Pro hard-51 pass@1 from 39.2% to 64.7% and Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 39.5% to 55.8%. The post New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65% appeared first on MarkTechPost .
content: Hugging Face’s harness-hub team has released Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted , a LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B . It was trained with reinforcement learning to work inside the pi coding agent . The Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted LoRA adapter targets one harness instead of general chat. For developers running local coding agents, that is the point. You keep the open base model and swap in a small, harness-specific adapter. TL;DR Size: LoRA rank 32 (alpha 64) on Qwen3.8-27B, a 27B dense hybrid with 262,144 native context. Merged BF16 checkpoint is about 54 GB. Runs on: vLLM with LoRA enabled, or llama.cpp with a GGUF adapter on a Q8_0 base. Inference VRAM is not disclosed. Training used 2x NVIDIA B200. Performance: Large pass@1 gains inside pi with thinking off, plus far shorter sessions. Best: 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), up from 39.2%. Worst: 55.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The base model with thinking already reaches 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro. Bottom line: Best: thinking-level accuracy at about 4.5x fewer tokens. Worst: small eval sets, self-reported, pi only. What is Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted? Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is a PEFT LoRA adapter that turns Qwen3.8-27B into a model tuned for pi. pi is an MIT-licensed agent toolkit with a coding agent CLI. The adapter is released under Apache-2.0 . It applies to the q, k, v, o, gate, up and down projections. It only works on Qwen3.8-27B. The base model is a dense hybrid . It alternates Gated DeltaNet linear-attention blocks with Gated Attention blocks across 64 layers. How does the harness adapter training work? The method comes from Hugging Face’s harness adapters post from November 6. The idea is 1 LoRA adapter per model and harness. Training runs inside the unmodified harness on verifiable tasks. For this checkpoint, the model card lists these details: Algorithm: AsyncGRPO from TRL , 8 rollouts per task at temperature 0.8. Tasks: 750 scale800 tasks interleaved with 300 TermGrade tasks. Reward: verifier correctness plus a tool-efficiency bonus with weight 0.1. Budget: up to 50 agent steps and 1,800 seconds per rollout, thinking off. Checkpoint: step 160. The run stopped at step 191 of 1,000 planned. Every tool call passes through safeagents , a rule-based proxy. It blocks calls such as fetching benchmark answers from the Hub. Blocked rollouts score 0, so RL pushes the model away from reward hacking. Benchmarks: how much does the LoRA adapter help? All numbers below are self-reported. They use the pi harness, 1 attempt per task. Benchmark (pi, thinking off) Base Qwen3.8-27B pi-adapted Change SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 39.2% 64.7% +25.5 ± 14.2 pts (p = 0.0023) Terminal-Bench 2.1 (86 tasks) 39.5% 55.8% +16.3 ± 9.1 pts (p = 0.0013) The adapter solved 15 new SWE-bench Pro tasks and lost 2. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, it gained 16 and lost 2. Efficiency is the larger story. On tasks both models solved, median turns fell from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, they fell from 18 to 8. The adapter also generates about 4.5x fewer tokens than the base model with thinking. && How does it compare with thinking mode and other adapters? With thinking on, the base model already scores 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro and 54.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. So the adapter matches thinking-level accuracy without paying for long reasoning traces. With thinking on, the adapter reaches 66.7% and 56.6%. Feature Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted Qwen3.8-27B base, thinking on Qwen3.8-27B-opencode-adapted bytkim/Qwen3.8-27B-pi Type LoRA r=32 Base model LoRA r=32 Full fine-tune, 28B Method AsyncGRPO RL None AsyncGRPO RL SFT then GRPO Harness pi pi OpenCode pi License Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 64.7% 64.7% 51.0% (OpenCode) Not disclosed Terminal-Bench 2.1 55.8% 54.2% 53.0% (OpenCode) Not disclosed Token use ~4.5x fewer than base + thinking Baseline ~6x to 8x fewer than base + thinking ~41% fewer output tokens (Terminal-Bench) Training hardware 2x B200 Not disclosed 2x B200 Not disclosed OpenCode adapter numbers use a different harness and are not directly comparable. How do you deploy it? The model card gives 4 routes: vLLM: serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B with --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 32 , thinking disabled. Point pi at http://localhost:8000/v1 . llama.cpp: load the GGUF adapter on a Q8_0 base GGUF. Llama.app on macOS: register the adapter with a 32,768-token context. Merge: merge with PEFT on CPU, then serve the 54 GB BF16 result without LoRA flags. Because adapters share 1 base model, a single server can host pi and OpenCode adapters side by side. Key Takeaways Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is an Apache-2.0, rank-32 RL LoRA for the pi agent. SWE-bench Pro hard-51 rises from 39.2% to 64.7%, thinking off. Median turns drop from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. It matches base-with-thinking accuracy at about 4.5x fewer tokens. Results are self-reported on small sets; the tweet’s 29.4% baseline was corrected.
